title: Stative Verbs in Everyday English
subtitle: A practical guide to states, changing meanings and natural -ing choices, with a light review of hobbies and preference language.

teacherNote.summary: The 29 August lesson is incorporated, the approved original platform style is preserved, stative verb coverage is broad, flashcards are English-only, and day-to-day state/action contrasts are interactive.

lessonNotes: A stative verb describes a condition, thought, feeling, sense, possession or relationship rather than an action in progress.
Stative meaning normally uses a simple tense: Mia knows the answer, Noah wants a break, and the camera belongs to Priya.
Some verbs can be stative or dynamic. The meaning decides the tense: I think it is useful expresses an opinion, while I am thinking about the problem describes a mental activity now.
Preference language from the previous lesson connects naturally with this topic: love, like, hate, prefer and want are usually stative, while enjoy is commonly followed by a noun or an -ing activity.
Useful hobby language remains in the practice: be crazy about, really like, quite like, do not mind, cannot stand, numismatics, birdwatching, memorabilia and photography.

grammar.title: The core pattern
grammar.rule: Use the present simple for a state that is true now or generally true. Do not add -ing just because the state is true at this moment.

grammar.title: Thoughts, opinions and knowledge
grammar.rule: Know, believe, understand, remember, mean, agree, doubt and think when it means have an opinion are usually stative.
examples: We think the plan is sensible.

grammar.title: Feelings, needs and preferences
grammar.rule: Love, like, dislike, hate, prefer, want, need, wish and mind usually describe an internal state, so the simple form is normal.

grammar.title: Senses and appearance
grammar.rule: See, hear, smell, taste, feel, seem, appear, look and sound are often stative when they describe passive perception or appearance.

grammar.title: Possession, connection and composition
grammar.rule: Have, own, possess, belong, contain, include, consist, involve and depend usually describe possession or relationships rather than actions.

grammar.title: Measurement, value and identity
grammar.rule: Cost, weigh, measure, fit, equal, matter, deserve, resemble, be and exist are commonly stative when they report a fact or condition.

grammar.title: When -ing becomes possible
grammar.rule: A normally stative verb can use a continuous form when it gains an active, temporary or deliberately changing meaning.
examples: Sam is being unusually patient today.

remember: Ask what the verb means in this sentence. If it names a state, fact, possession, opinion or passive sense, choose the simple form. If it names an activity happening around now, the continuous form may be correct.
watchOut: Marketing and very informal speech sometimes use forms such as I am loving it. Learn the standard pattern first: I love it. Also remember that have can be continuous for activities such as having lunch, but not for possession: I have a fast car.

dailyUsage.actionExample: I am thinking about joining the club.
dailyUsage.tip: Do not say I am thinking it is relaxing when you simply mean this is my opinion.

dailyUsage.actionMeaning: take part in an activity or experience
dailyUsage.actionExample: Nadia is having lunch with a collector.
dailyUsage.tip: Meals, showers, lessons and a good time can be activities; possession cannot.

dailyUsage.actionExample: I am seeing the dentist tomorrow.
dailyUsage.tip: The continuous form changes see from passive perception to an arranged or repeated meeting.

dailyUsage.actionExample: The chef is tasting the tea.
dailyUsage.tip: The tea is not doing an action; the chef is.

dailyUsage.actionExample: Ravi is smelling the bread to check it.
dailyUsage.tip: Smell is dynamic when someone actively uses their nose.

dailyUsage.stateMeaning: have an opinion, emotion or physical condition
dailyUsage.stateExample: I feel tired after the trip.
dailyUsage.actionExample: Mira is feeling the fabric for a rough patch.
dailyUsage.tip: I am feeling tired is possible when emphasising a temporary experience, but I feel tired is the safe everyday choice.

dailyUsage.actionExample: Leo is looking at the camera.
dailyUsage.tip: Look meaning appear is followed by an adjective; look at names an action.

dailyUsage.stateMeaning: describe identity or a usual quality
dailyUsage.actionMeaning: behave temporarily in a particular way
dailyUsage.actionExample: Ana is being very patient today.
dailyUsage.tip: Being plus an adjective usually highlights temporary behaviour, not a permanent trait.

dailyUsage.actionExample: The assistant is weighing the parcel.
dailyUsage.tip: The object has a weight; a person or machine performs the measuring action.

reading.title: A Busy Saturday at the Curiosity Club
reading.text:
The Curiosity Club meets in a bright room above the town library. Its members have very different hobbies, but they all believe that a good question can connect people. This Saturday, the club is holding a small open day for new visitors.

At the first table, Hana is showing a collection of concert memorabilia. The display contains old tickets, posters and a drumstick from a local band. She owns the tickets, but the drumstick belongs to her brother. A visitor thinks the drumstick looks ordinary, yet Hana knows its story matters. She explains where it came from and asks the visitor which music he prefers.

Across the room, Felix has a numismatics display. One silver coin weighs only a few grams and costs less than a modern lunch, but it is still his favourite. He loves researching the people shown on coins. At the moment, he is weighing a new coin because he wants to compare it with the information in a catalogue. The coin weighs twelve grams, so the result appears correct.

Near the window, Priya is preparing tea for the visitors. She tastes the first cup and adds a little lemon. The tea now tastes fresher. She is also thinking about joining the photography group, although she thinks a new camera is too expensive. Leo, a street photographer, tells her that a phone camera is enough to begin.

The open day works because the members do more than describe objects. They listen to each visitor, react to one detail and ask a follow-up question. By the end, Priya quite likes the idea of street photography, while Leo is thinking about starting a small ticket collection. Their interests are changing, but the grammar makes each meaning clear.

listening.title: State or Action at the Hobby Fair?
listening.instructions: Listen once for the situation. Listen again for the exact verb forms. Then unlock the transcript and check your answers.
listening.script:
Maya: This photography fair looks busy. Do you know anyone here?
Leo: Yes. I know Sam, the man near the entrance. He owns the vintage camera stall.
Maya: I think his cameras look beautiful, but they cost a lot.
Leo: True. I am thinking about buying a smaller one.
Maya: What is Nina doing beside the café?
Leo: She is tasting three kinds of tea for her food blog. She says the green tea tastes best.
Maya: I see. Are you seeing Sam later?
Leo: Yes, I am seeing him at six to discuss a photography walk. He really likes street photography, and I quite like it too.

questions.q: Who owns the vintage camera stall?

questions.why: Am thinking about shows active consideration.

questions.q: What does the green tea tastes best describe?
What does Leo mean by I am seeing him at six?
opt: He can notice Sam with his eyes.
questions.why: See can be dynamic when it means meet.
